problem: The chapter gives only 'contiguous addresses' as the condition for one summary prefix. Contiguity alone is not enough: the block must also be aligned, that is, it must have a power-of-two size and start at a multiple of that size. A student who follows the stated rule could wrongly 'aggregate' 10.0.1.0/24 to 10.0.4.0/24 (contiguous) into a /22 such as 10.0.1.0/22, which is not a valid network address for a /22 and does not cover the four networks cleanly.
fix: State the full condition: a set of prefixes aggregates into one summary only if the block is contiguous, its size is a power of two, and the first address is a multiple of the block size (all common bits identical). The chapter's 10.0.0.0–10.0.3.0 and 172.16.4.0–172.16.7.0 examples satisfy this; mention that an unaligned set needs a more general (less specific) prefix plus exception routes.

problem: 'Default route' is used twice (table row 'Best use: Stub, small, default route'; Q6 answer 'A single default static route works') but is never defined. A first-time reader does not know it means the 0.0.0.0/0 entry that matches every destination when no longer prefix matches.
fix: Define it at first use: a default route is the prefix 0.0.0.0/0 (all zero prefix bits), which matches every destination and acts as the last-resort entry when no longer prefix matches.

problem: The rule is stated only for the case where several entries match. It does not say what happens when no entry matches, which students often ask and which ties directly to the default route mentioned later.
fix: Add one sentence: if no entry matches (and there is no default route), the router drops the packet and may send an ICMP destination-unreachable message back to the source.
